No prosodic correlates of this status as a word head has however been identified so far.2 Now that we have laid out some basic facts concerning the tonal system of Bàsàá, let us turn to two major tonal processes, which are the main source of contour tones and downstepped H tones: High Tone Spreading ... [p.169] In contrast with many of its relatives, Bàsàá does not have a general restriction on tone contours; both falling (HL) and rising (LH) contours are allowed . Tonal contours are however restricted to bimoraic syllables, suggesting that the mora (and ... [p.170] Bisyllabic word stems exhibit the four surface tonal patterns illustrated in (8) to (11) respectively: HH, LH, LL, and H - HL (Hyman, 2003) .
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had
sweep_summary: Basaa (basa1284) is not in the catalog. The search of works with stress or accent in the title had one item, Makasso 2010 'Processus de relativisation en bàsàa: de la syntaxe à la prosodie' (ZASPiL 53:145-158, doi:10.21248/zaspil.53.2010.396). It was already held by the project from our earlier reading; I re-downloaded it from the ZASPiL download endpoint (byte-identical), confirmed the bibliographic record on the journal landing page, and read it in full. It is about relative-clause morphosyntax and Intonational-Phrase phrasing (tonal realisation of /wɛ̀/, pauses) in a two-tone language; it contains no term for or statement about word stress/accent. Relevance: prosody-but-not-word-stress; priority none; a line was appended to there. The best stress-relevant first-hand statement available held by the project remains Makasso, Hamlaoui & Lee 2016 pp. chapter closed-access): 'No automatic prominence on the penultimate or final vowel is observed in Bàsàá'; stem-initial syllable is at most a segmentally-defined word head with no prosodic correlates identified. direct download/automated download were used instead.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Basaa is a tone language (underlying H vs L; surface H, L, downstepped H, HL, LH; contours only on bimoraic syllables). The authors (first author a native-speaker linguist) state there is no automatic penultimate or final prominence; the only candidate for word-level prominence is the stem-initial (root-initial) syllable, which licenses the fullest segmental contrasts and is treated as the word's head following Hyman 2003, but no phonetic/prosodic stress correlate of that status has been identified. I.e. no demonstrable word stress; if any accent, it is stem-initial and evidenced distributionally, not phonetically.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Related evidence: Idiatov & Van de Velde 2016 (slides, saved) report instrumental stem-initial consonant lengthening in their NW Bantu sample including Basaa; Downing 2004:123-124 (saved) analyses Basaa C1>C2>C3 consonant-contrast asymmetries (Hyman 1990, 2000) as stem-initial accent; Hyman 2008:331-333 (saved) calls it a stem-initial 'strength' asymmetry without claiming stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prosodic stem = root + suffixes; prefixes outside). Phrase level: High Tone Spreading within phonological phrases, Falling Tone Simplification blocked at Intonation Phrase left edges; no obligatory final lowering (Hamlaoui & Szendrői 2017). Makasso 2008:54-55 argues Basaa has no intonational structure independent of tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern prosodic sources (Makasso, Hamlaoui, Lee) rest on data from Emmanuel-Moselly Makasso, a native speaker of the Northern variety of Bàsàá (per Hamlaoui & Szendrői 2017 fn.6); this is standard Basaa = basa1284, no separate dialect glottocode needed. Schürle 1912 describes 'Basa' of the German colonial period (same language, pre-tonal analysis).

tone_statements.quote: Bàsàá is a tonal language with a three-way underlying opposition between H(igh), L(ow) and toneless (∅) tone-bearing units (TBUs) (Dimmendaal 1988; Hyman 2003; Makasso 2008 and in particular Bitjaa Kody 1993; Hamlaoui et al. 2014; Makasso et al. 2016 on toneless TBUs). As a result of a number of tonal processes, Bàsàá’s surface realizations contrast H, L, LH (rising), HL (falling) and ꜜH (‘downstepped’ H) tones. ... Floating L tones are also pretty common in Bàsàá, some of them clearly resulting from a historical loss of segments.

sources.quote: Une caractéristique importante des relatives en bàsàa est leur organisation prosodique, en particulier le fait que leur frontière droite coïncide avec la fin d'un Groupe Intonatif. [...] La finale de Groupe Intonatif est, entre autres marquées par des réalisations tonales caractéristiques. [...] En bàsàa les Groupes Intonatifs sont également séparés par des pauses. (pp.154-156) [EN: An important characteristic of relatives in Bàsàa is their prosodic organisation, in particular the fact that their right edge coincides with the end of an Intonational Phrase. The IP end is marked, among other things, by characteristic tonal realisations. In Bàsàa IPs are also separated by pauses.]
sources.locator: whole paper read (14 pp. = ZASPiL 53:145-158); prosody section 4 'Prosodie des relatives', pp.154-156
sources.note: Nothing. The paper is a morphosyntactic sketch of relative clauses (demonstrative strategy, locative, restrictive vs non-restrictive, definiteness) plus a short prosody section showing that the right edge of a relative is an Intonational-Phrase boundary, diagnosed by the tonal realisation of the 2sg pronoun /wɛ̀/ (lexical L, H after the verb, falling contour IP-finally) and by pauses (97% of cases in the two-speaker read corpus). The words accent, stress, proéminence, intensité, tonique do not occur anywhere in the text (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text). Silent on word stre…

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Yabassi, a Bantu language spoken in the Littoral province of Cameroon and classified in Guthrie under A40, that is, as a dialect of Basaa, is such a language (Guthrie 1967). It has three level tones, the high (H), the low (L) and the mid tone (M). [...] A less studied phenomenon is the case of languages without the usual downstep but which exhibit downdrift, that is, the automatic lowering of a high tone after a linked low tone.
sources.locator: p. 77, introduction; abstract same page: 'three level surface tones (high, mid, and low); The high tone downdrifts after a low tone.'
sources.note: This work describes Yabassi (the paper's own label; p. 77: 'a Bantu language spoken in the Littoral province of Cameroon and classified in Guthrie under A40, that is, as a dialect of Basaa').Tone only; the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur in the paper. System stated: three level surface tones H, M, L; downdrift of H after L, no downstep (p. 77); analysis in features [upper]/[raised] with M either default [-upper +raised] on toneless TBUs or lexical H plus floating L (pp. 77-78, 86).
